extracted.intended_audience: citizens of New York and readers interested in the proposed Constitution and federal union
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/persuasive essays (Federalist-style) arguing for a strong federal Union by enumerating the practical dangers of disunion and the benefits of consolidation. Focuses on causes of interstate conflict, military/financial consequences, and political theory (e.g., Montesquieu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from territorial disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsettled Western territory, discordant and undecided claims between States, and the absence of a common umpire would revive and multiply land-claims after dissolution of the Union. Cessions to the United States presently make amicable termination more likely; disunion would prompt reclamation, competing principles of apportionment, and likely resort to the sword (examples: Connecticut–Pennsylvania Wyoming dispute; controversy with Vermont).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial competition as source of contention
rubrics_metrics.description: The competitions of commerce would be another fruitful source of contention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If States pursue separate commercial policies they will create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions that beget discontent. Habits of intercourse based on equal privileges sharpen resentment when neighbors adopt protectionist or preferential measures. Infractions and efforts to repel them lead to reprisals and war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of tributary relations via commercial regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The opportunities which some States would have of rendering others tributary to them by commercial regulations would be impatiently submitted to by the tributary States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York laying duties that in effect tax Connecticut and New Jersey consumers. Neighboring states would resent paying duties that benefit a metropolis; inability to distinguish customers in shared markets would make such arrangements inflammatory and likely provoke resistance or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debt apportionment and its corrosive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial apportionment and subsequent extinguishment of debt would produce ill-humor and animosity—few apportionment rules are free from objection. Divergent principles on discharging debt, differences in creditor/debtor concentration, real resource deficiencies, mismanagement, and reluctance to fund obligations all generate delinquencies, recriminations, and risk of internal disorder; foreign creditors add external pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws violating private contracts provoke inter-state retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws in violation of private contracts, as they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them, may be considered as another probable source of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative acts upsetting contracted rights can be viewed as aggressions, producing retaliation (example: Connecticut’s resentment over Rhode Island’s legislative 'enormities'). Without federal restraint, such breaches could lead to war 'not of PARCHMENT, but of the sword.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatible foreign alliances entangle states and invite exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of incompatible alliances between the different States or confederacies and different foreign nations ... would, by the operation of such jarring alliances, be gradually entangled in all the pernicious labyrinths of European politics and wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disunion would allow foreign powers to play parts against American parts (divide et impera), making the parts prey to artifices and machinations of external enemies; a strong Union reduces exposure to such manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: War in a disunited America would favor standing armies and executive aggrandizement
rubrics_metrics.description: War between the States ... would be accompanied with much greater distresses ... Frequent war and constant apprehension ... will infallibly produce [standing armies].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a disunited situation, weaker States would raise disciplined armies and fortifications to match stronger neighbors, strengthening executive power and tipping constitutions toward monarchy. Standing armies elevate the military above civil institutions and erode liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of fortifications and militia traditions makes warfare predatory
rubrics_metrics.description: In this country the scene would be altogether reversed ... The want of fortifications, leaving the frontiers of one state open to another, would facilitate inroads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the U.S. lacked European-style fortifications and professional armies, conquests would be easy to make and hard to retain, leading to desultory, predatory wars with plunder and devastation concentrated on individuals rather than decisive territorial gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as barrier against faction and insurrection (enlargement of sphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm Union will be of the utmost moment to the peace and liberty of the States, as a barrier against domestic faction and insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enlarging the orbit (a larger republic or confederacy) mitigates the vices of small republics by distributing power, introducing checks and balances, and making factional projects less likely to succeed. The confederate republic can suppress faction, reform abuses, and prevent single-member usurpation; larger scale aids internal tranquillity and external security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Montesquieu’s concept of a confederate republic
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu’s idea: a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC is a convention by which several smaller STATES agree to become members of a larger ONE ... A republic of this kind ... may support itself without any internal corruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted approval: such a confederacy combines internal republican advantages with external force like monarchy; it prevents usurpation by diffusing power, allows confederates to quell insurrections in one member, and preserves sovereignty of members while gaining collective security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between confederacy and consolidation is not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction ... has been raised between a CONFEDERACY and a CONSOLIDATION of the States ... These positions are, in the main, arbitrary; they are supported neither by principle nor precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal authority's extent and modifications are discretionary; so long as state organizations remain for local purposes, a broad federal sovereignty that includes direct senatorial representation and reserved state powers still fits the idea of a confederacy. Examples (e.g., Lycian confederacy) show historical practice varied and sometimes intrusive on local administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical example: Lycian confederacy shows federal interference can exist
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Lycian confederacy ... the COMMON COUNCIL had the appointment of all the judges and magistrates of the respective CITIES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical example illustrates that confederacies have often exercised significant authority over members’ internal administration, undermining any rigid rule that confederacies must never touch domestic institutions; such precedents inform constitutional design choices.
